lessons.subject: history_geography
lessons.lesson_title: Early Peloponnesian War: Strategy, Long Walls, and Plague
lessons.previous_learning: Day 14 history was strong on multi-cause reasoning about why war began.
lessons.course_context: Advance from causes to early-war strategy and consequences.
learning_objectives: Compare Spartan land strength with Athenian naval strength.
Explain Long Walls and Periclean strategy.
Analyze the strategy trade-off and plague.
lessons.why_it_matters: History explains interactions among geography, choices, strengths, and unexpected events.

vocabulary.definition: a benefit gained while accepting a cost

lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: Sparta was strongest on land; Athens at sea. Pericles avoided a major land battle, used the Long Walls and naval supply, and kept many people inside Athens. This reduced exposure to Spartan land power but increased crowding; plague then caused enormous human and political damage.

worked_examples.title: Strategy
worked_examples.explanation: A rational strategy reduces exposure to enemy advantage.

worked_examples.title: Trade-off
worked_examples.problem: Long Walls protect what and risk what?
worked_examples.explanation: A strategy can solve one problem while worsening another.

worked_examples.title: Plague
worked_examples.solution: Deaths plus loss of leadership, morale, manpower, stability.

independent_practice.prompt: Why did Athens avoid a major open land battle?
How did Long Walls and Piraeus help Athens resist?
Explain one benefit and one cost of Pericles’s strategy.
Why did plague damage more than population?
Build: Spartan invasion -> Athenian response -> crowding -> plague impact.
Was Pericles’s strategy foolish because plague happened? Defend carefully.

exit_ticket.prompt: In 5 sentences explain how Athenian strengths, Spartan strengths, and plague shaped the early war.
exit_ticket.answer: Contrast land/naval strength, explain Long Walls/naval supply, and show how plague undermined Athens.

lessons.voice_prompt: Teach before questioning. Speak directly to Atticus. Use whiteboard_draw to make a simple map with ATHENS, PIRAEUS, LONG WALLS, SEA, and a Spartan land force; add arrows for land pressure and sea supply. Then draw a two-column trade-off: protection from land invasion / crowding and disease risk. Do not draw assigned answers.

lessons.subject: literature
lessons.lesson_title: The Balcony Light: Perspective, Tone, and Nuance
lessons.previous_learning: Day 14 literature was strong, but completeness still needs monitoring.
lessons.course_context: Advance into perspective, tone, and nuanced interpretation.
lessons.why_it_matters: Advanced reading separates evidence from interpretation and notices revision of thought.
lessons.written_instruction: Read The Balcony Light. Separate neutral facts from Nadia’s and Marcus’s interpretations and notice Nadia’s tone shift after repeated timing evidence.

worked_examples.title: Fact vs perspective
worked_examples.problem: Power fails after balcony lights come on.
worked_examples.solution: Timing is fact; cause is interpretation.

independent_practice.prompt: What fact do both characters observe?
What does “That proves nothing” reveal about Nadia’s attitude?
How does Nadia’s final tone differ?
Why is the final explanation more nuanced?
Write a theme about evidence and changing your mind.
Give two supporting details and significance.

exit_ticket.prompt: Explain fact vs character perspective in one sentence.
exit_ticket.answer: A fact is what happens; perspective is how someone interprets it.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. If useful, use whiteboard_draw for a three-column table FACT / NADIA INTERPRETS / MARCUS INTERPRETS. Only neutral facts go in the first column. Never answer assigned questions. If he gives plot instead of significance, ask what the detail proves or reveals.

lessons.subject: writing
lessons.previous_learning: Day 14 showed strong reasoning but incomplete requested formats and some vague wording.
lessons.course_context: Require precise evidence-reasoning pairs and visible revision.
learning_objectives: Complete a full paragraph and conclusion.
lessons.why_it_matters: Strong writing is revised, not merely first-draft correct.
lessons.written_instruction: Atticus: a correct idea is only the start. After every evidence sentence ask: What does this prove? Then revise vague words and incomplete reasoning.

worked_examples.title: Weak vs strong
worked_examples.problem: Marcus turns on balcony lights and power fails.
worked_examples.solution: Repeated timing supports the load idea while the cracked cable may also matter.
worked_examples.explanation: Strong reasoning explains what evidence proves without oversimplifying.

independent_practice.prompt: Improve: Nadia was stubborn. Use one exact line/action.
Make “Both were right because there were two causes” precise.
Write 7-9 sentences: Why is Nadia’s final explanation stronger? Use two exact details, reasoning, conclusion.

exit_ticket.prompt: Complete revision pass: claim, two evidence items, reasoning, replace one vague word, sentence boundaries, conclusion.

lessons.voice_prompt: Speak directly to Atticus. Do not dictate sentences. If vague, identify the vague word. If reasoning repeats evidence, ask what the detail proves. Use whiteboard_draw only for a different CLAIM -> EVIDENCE -> REASONING example, not his assigned paragraph.
